utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Indah Susanti for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Tatjana Savic -- Ms. Tatjana Savic and we have two interns with us, Ms. Amanda Gruenhagen and Mr. Fernando Dutra appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, we have been alerted by the Court Officer that there are one or two housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as we are concerned, it was just to remove the MFI status from the document which has been marked 2358. We understand the Defence accept it was disclosed to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the MFI qualification is removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other matter was, of course, the Sarajevo CSB chart was taken off by the witness but I think I'll have to wait until he comes in to find out if he wants to make any alterations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Tusevljak. Before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you of your solemn declaration. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Tusevljak, you took away the diagram of the CSB Sarajevo. So can I ask whether you want to make any alterations to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we better have it up on the screen. It's 2355 MFI? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you say there's any information there which is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered some corrections there in relation to who was a member of the Security Services Centre and for how long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So it's just dates, is it, that you wanted to alter?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the dates. Not all of them were inspectors also, some were mere employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said that before. Can you just -- I think we needed to remove the word "inspector" from the forensic crime technicians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we possibly zoom in, please, on the left-hand side of this chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wonder if I may propose that we put it on the ELMO the copy that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- made the alterations and then he can explain what alterations he made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That seems a very sensible idea. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then after it was accepted, then you can reload the new version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I am afraid your writing, we discovered from when we were given it, is not the easiest to read. Could you just tell us please what you've written by the side of Mr. Rakic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says he was never a member of the Security Services Centre. He was with the Rajlovac police station right from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was at Rajlovac, you say, and was never an inspector in the CSB? All right. We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Pekic, he was a member of your staff, though?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think only in April. After that he went over to the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic came sometime in July 1992. However, as soon as late 1992 he went to the MUP school in Banja Luka. As a matter of fact he still works there. So he was with the school from day one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, he did come to work for you in July 1992 and when do you say he went to the school? Oh, late 1992. All right.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as late 1992, when the school was first established. That should be easy enough to verify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic arrived in October 1992, but early 1993 or thereabouts, he was appointed chief at the Novo Sarajevo public security station leaving my own station. I think his name is displayed on the diagram of chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Don't worry about that because we are only interested in what it looked like during 1992. Mr. Sakota?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Sakota left for the Banja Luka public security centre as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but when?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992. I don't know the exact date but he too left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But at some stage do you agree that from August 1992 he was working in the CSB and at some later stage went to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as inspector, from August on he was a white collar crime inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. What do you say about Mr. -- the last one on that list? Mr. Janjetovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between June and the end of war, he was with the crime police of the Security Services Centre working as a white collar crime inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, between June and the end of?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1995. The end of war. He was with the crime police department working as a chief of the white collar crime department, or unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you mean he wasn't in -- he was in the CSB but not as part of your unit?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was chief of the white collar crime unit and the forensics unit in the centre, and the general crime unit. There were a total of three.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, I am sorry, what is the problem with him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said there was a problem. I said he was there between July and the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to know where you say it's inaccurate. I don't need to know how long these people were working there, provided they were working through 1992. Going to Mr. Lazic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savka Lazic, she worked from the very beginning with the RS MUP, the crime police administration. So she was not one of my people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She didn't work for you, she was administration. All right. So she's out, you say. Mr. Tesanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tesanovic, forensic technician, crime forensic technician. Not an inspector, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about the next one, you've written something about Mr. Bozovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as 1993 he went to the material and financial affairs department, what we called the mat fin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look. Listen for a moment, would you. I -- provided they worked there in 1992, that's all I'm concerned about. Don't worry about what happened to them in 1993. What about the lady at -- oh, she was a typist, is there any problem with her?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but she too left in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember when?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now what about the third -- sorry, the fourth line down, are you just complaining there that none of these people were inspectors, or what?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [Indiscernible] were KDZ anti-sabotage detection, that's what it means. They all went to the RS MUP as early as July 1992. So in actual fact they were with us up until July that year. Sekula Micic likewise was not with us. He was with the RS MUP the whole time. The one thing missing in this diagram is Zoran Glusac who came sometime in August 1992. And Zoran Sedanovic who also arrived in the latter half of 1992 to work as a general crime inspector. Another lad, Stankovic, I can't remember his first name, came to the anti-sabotage department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You've written something right at the -- you've written those two names that we can see, what is the last thing you've written on that diagram?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, he just said, that's Stankovic, KDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He explained that. But I think you missed the first one, Sasa Blagojevic, there is a note there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The very first one on the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us what that says?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1992 he was in Gorazde for about two months and then as soon as he came back, he left for Zvornik. After that he left the RS MUP. And all of this happened in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying Sasa Blagojevic never worked for the CSB Sarajevo as one of your inspectors?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only for that brief period when he was in Zvornik, and he went there because his wife was pregnant. For family reasons, in other words. So I didn't hear from him that often when he was in Zvornik, although formally he worked with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So he may have been -- you are saying he was based in Zvornik but he was actually one of your employees -- or one of your inspectors?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was on my list, but that was more intended to keep him from being drafted by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we just go over to right side of the diagram for a moment. Staying at the top, please. Yes, just there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was in charge of the department for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's very difficult to read and I haven't got a copy here. No, to the -- slightly to the left, to the left, the left, please. Thank you, stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the department for analysis and information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a special unit run by the chief of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but who was in charge of that department? The name, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either Savo Sarac or Mihajlo Bajic. I'm not sure which of the two. They are not included in this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I know because we had some difficulty in finding who this was. What about number 7, mat fin, or material finances. Do you know who was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first Nikola Lopatic, and he was followed by Bozovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I suppose just to complete it, do you happen to remember who was in charge of the fire department?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a single inspector there, Danilo Prove. He was both chief and inspector, simply because there was no one else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what we'll do is we'll check the information against our sources and if we agree that what he says is correct, we will re-alter the plan and then ask for it to be admitted in full. Leave it as an MFI for the moment, and as Mr. Zecevic suggested, replace it with a new chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have just a copy of the -- disclose the copy of the document which the witness has made the alteration, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll photocopy -- can we have it back now and we'll arrange for photocopies to be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to return for one last time, Mr. Tusevljak, to when Novo Sarajevo SJB came into existence. Yesterday when I put it to you that it was on the 5th of April and I said it was a take-over, you said it was never taken over because it moved into a different building, but it wasn't the 5th of April. And at page 22516, I asked you: "When did, in your opinion, the Novo Sarajevo station -- Novo Sarajevo Serbian MUP SJB come into existence?" And you said: "Sometime in mid-April." I'd like you to have a look, please, now at a document which is -- it's been given the 65 ter number 20212.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we have a tab?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 62. Your Honours, it was added last night.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report on the operation of Novo Sarajevo SJB dated the 27th of December, sent to your CSB, and presumably at some stage you would have seen this, Mr. Tusevljak, or at least it would have been discussed at one of your collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably saw him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Saw it, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if he was there at the collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, it's signed by Mr. Mihajlovic, if we go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can be given the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go then, please, back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Novo Sarajevo SJB was formed on the 5th of April, 1992, so do now accept that that is when it came into existence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree about the date, the 5th of April. On the 5th of April, the school building at Vrace was taken by the MUP. It says here that on the 5th of April, it was established with its seat at the former centre for staff training in Vrace. So, in actual fact, could it have been established in the staff training centre before the building itself was taken, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was the day, as you told us, it was over the night of the 4th to the 5th of April that the Vrace school was seized, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we spoke about the 4th and 5th of April, we spoke about when it was taken by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League, the public security station in Novo Sarajevo, I mean. And that's what we were talking about, about the Novo Sarajevo public security station also when we spoke about the murder of police officer Pero Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, my fault.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the school was actually taken over by the forces of the Serbian MUP, in particular Mr. Karisik and other people, on the night of the 4th to the 5th of April, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that didn't happen that night. It happened in broad daylight on the 5th of April, I think sometime in the afternoon. It was past noon, I'm certain about that. I wasn't myself at Vrace but I know that this happened in broad daylight and not under cover of the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So for whatever reason, Mr. Mihajlovic has either deliberately put a wrong date or made a mistake. And you are absolutely right because it says it was established in four different locations, Grbavica, Vrace, Lukavica, and the Vrace educational centre. And just further on this, police officers of the Vrace police detachment were engaged in traffic control at the post on the intersection of, that must be Bosanski Surbat Street -- and I can say Bjelosevic but this one, Bjelopoljska Street, and they held the position on the Jewish cemetery line; that is, they were constantly involved in combat operations. Is that accurate as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was disclosed. It's an earlier disclosed document and I ask that it be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have the objection on the same basis as I articulated yesterday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, could you assist us as to why you are seeking to tender this, is it merely the question of the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, there's two matters. Firstly the date and where the station was, and secondly, the activities of the part of the Novo Sarajevo police station at the Jewish cemetery for a reason that will become apparent a little later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can suggest then that we -- that the document be MFI'd until we see the reason which will become apparent later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would adopt Mr. Zecevic's suggestion and mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2359, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to return briefly to the question of communications which we discussed at some length yesterday, Mr. Tusevljak. At page 2272 -- sorry, 22272 of your evidence, which would have been on Thursday of last week, you stated that all the communications with all the police stations in the territory of the Birac region were severed. You were asked by Mr. Zecevic could you list the stations that you were referring to, and you said Skelani, Bratunac, Zvornik, Milici, Sekovici, and you said the communications were cut off. Now -- and at a later stage you said that you had never received any information towards Zvornik until you had the meeting in the 26th of July with the heads of the crime departments. Now, first, are you actually asserting that it was impossible for any of those police stations to be reached?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically one could reach the stations, that is, it was possible to drive there. We were talking about communications. For instance, if I want to send a dispatch, there used to be a procedure in the MUP and one of my employees would take this dispatch to the communication centre and then it would be dispatched further on. So that used to be the standard procedure in the police. At the time if there were any similar dispatches, they would have to be taken there, so to speak, on foot. If somebody would happen to go that way, he would take the dispatch. I think that at the time there was no organised courier service, so I spoke about the problems related to communications. I didn't mean to say that it was physically impossible to reach those police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Because at this time even early on, the telephones were still working, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Telephones from Lukavica were cut off. The only phones that were functioning at the time were the phones at Pale - just one minute - and in Lukavica because the switchboard was in Sarajevo and it burned on the 2nd of May, or thereabouts. Then it was possible to communicate only locally from that point on. And I can tell you that all the way until the end of war, I could not call anybody outside that area unless I used the phone in the chief of the -- in the office of the chief of the centre because there was a hot line that used some other routing and sometimes we were able to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come back to that, but was that a hot line that enabled the chief of the centre to reach MUP headquarters and other police stations, other SJBs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think it was only for communicating with the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Because the military -- I see what you mean. You could route a call through the military communications installations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe the chief was able to do that. We were not able to do that. It was his link with the corps command and the commanders of the brigade -- brigades. I don't know what the level was and I don't know whether he was able to use this line for some other purposes. I myself never used this line in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've just said, "and I can tell you that all the way until the end of the war, I could not call anybody outside that area unless I used the phone in the chief's office ..." So from that, we understood that you did use the phone. Are you now saying you never used it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a matter of incorrect interpretation. I said that I did not use the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You did now. All right. But, I'm sorry, going back to the original point I started before you mentioned the hot line --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just establish the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said telephones in Lukavica were cut off. You didn't move to Lukavica until July, did you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Lukavica in July. But the same situation was also in the school at Vrace. There were almost no telephones there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But is that right, because when the school was taken over didn't you have all the equipment taken over that belonged to the school? You had telephones, didn't you, at Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I arrived at Vrace sometime in mid-May, not before that. So what kind of equipment was found there and what were the capabilities in April, I really don't know. I'm only talking about the time when I began working in the Security Services Centre and I'm only talking about what I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tusevljak. You arrived in May. Are you saying that when you got there in May there was no capability of making telephone calls from Vrace?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe there were some phones in the communication centre itself. But there were no phones that worked in our offices. We didn't have the possibility to call anybody else except maybe Lukavica, I think the numbers began with 4 or 6, so we could only call that far.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that period, Mr. Stanisic, the minister, was also based at Vrace, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the headquarters of the MUP was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You say you didn't know about intercepts during the period but you found out about them since through your new job. Are you aware that there are a number of intercepted conversations coming from Vraca to various places and likewise from various places to Vraca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I know it now and I know that it pertains only to one line, one telephone number that was in the communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So you obviously studied them quite carefully. So clearly there was at least one telephone in operation at Vraca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. That's what I saw from the intercept. But at the time I did not have access to that phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't just walk into the MUP or the communication centre just like that simply to say I wanted to make a phone call.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: An official phone call, why not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably had no need at the time to request an official phone call. With whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's different. It's no good making these assertions, Mr. Tusevljak, unless you actually tried and failed. If you never tried to make a phone call, then you have no idea what telephone equipment was available, have you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that I don't know. We spoke about one phone. I read some of the intercepts simply because I had a chance to read those intercepts in relation to my current job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that. All right. I don't want to pursue this. Can we just for a moment return to Zvornik. You later said that you had -- that Zvornik, which came under the CSB Sarajevo, you never received any communications from them. Isn't it right that, in fact, originally Zvornik was attached to the CSB Bijeljina and then was altered to Sarajevo officially?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the centre was in Bijeljina and when it was returned to Sarajevo. I think that our centre was called Romanija-Birac and the name was chosen precisely because it comprised a police station within the area of Romanija and the area of Birac, and Zvornik is in the area of Birac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could you have a look, please, at a couple of documents which predate your meeting in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, could we have up P329 which is at tab 4D.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's a document dated the 3rd of June, addressed to the Security Services Centre in Bijeljina, responding to a document, in fact, from you of the 16th of May -- sorry, from you, I mean the Sarajevo Security Services Centre, "pursuant to the aforementioned document, we submit here with a daily report on the current and security-related incidents on the 2nd of June," territory of Zvornik which is to be forwarded to the Sarajevo CSB. I don't know whether -- would you have got copies of the daily reports or seen the daily reports that came from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, my service did not receive those daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So when you said there was no communication with Zvornik, what you are saying is that you, your service did not get reports from them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there were no communications whatsoever. You can see it from this. If you read this document, you can clearly see that the public security station -- centre in Sarajevo sent a document on the 15th of June [as interpreted] and the reply by the public security station was sent on the 3rd of June. So it's 17 days between the two events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's 16th of May, not 15th of June. Line 10 -- 9 and 10, 17. Page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's when there was -- this was an instruction, wasn't it, I think we may have it somewhere, I have to look for it, that went out to all security stations explaining that there should be daily reports sent on the security situation; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I have to explain a few things here, if I am permitted to do so?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document drafted by the public security station in Zvornik, if it arrived in the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo, if it arrived. Here where you find the number in this corner, it was Zoran Cvijetic, the chief of the centre, who wrote Drago, Simo, Bajic and this would confirm that the document actually reached the chief of the centre. And we see no such thing on this document. Maybe you'll recall that when the Defence showed me some documents, I would always read out whatever was written in the upper corner. So it is not possible established from this document that it ever reached the Security Services Centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well let's have a look at the next one, shall we, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Document 3 -- Exhibit 330, which is at tab 4E.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The last one we saw sent the daily report on the 3rd for the events of the 2nd of June. This one is dated the 4th of June, and does that have a stamp on it showing that it was received apparently by Bijeljina on the 4th of June at 10.36?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's no Sarajevo here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So your assertion is, is it, that there's no evidence that these documents from Zvornik ever reached the CSB at Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that. I merely explained that a document arriving in the Security Services Centre, just like this one, has the stamp confirming that it arrived in Bijeljina. Somebody would put the same kind of stamp at the communication in Vrace or later on in Lukavica. And when the document reaches the chief of the centre, who received all the mail arriving to all the departments, he would normally initial it and he would leave some trace signifying who was in charge of processing that mail. Or if it didn't reach him, then there would be no initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, for the clarity of this document, can you just direct the witness to read the stamp on the right side. Who received this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've said Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but who in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The National Defence Secretariat, according to the translation. Is that right, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says National Defence Secretariat, which means that they were the ones who received this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, of course it depends where the copy comes from, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we go back to the previous document for a moment, which is 329. Exhibit P329. Can we highlight the fax at the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you read what that says, Mr. Tusevljak, please? You may have to go a bit --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can see here tells me that it was sent to the fax number 0758 and so on from the number that begins with 076. I wouldn't know what was the receiving fax and what was the sending fax. I think it was Zvornik. I think this used to be the area code for Zvornik and Tuzla, while 076 was the area code of Bijeljina. The area code of Sarajevo was 071.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So it's sent out -- it's originally sent to the fax number 075; is that right? Because we can see the time 12.19, and then apparently it's sent on to a different number beginning 076 at 12.25. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So clearly some communications existed, didn't they, even in June, the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we cannot see the existence of any communication with Sarajevo. This testifies to the communication between Zvornik and Bijeljina, but we cannot find Sarajevo anywhere here and we are talking about the Sarajevo centre, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You understand of course, don't you, Mr. Tusevljak, because of your experience in investigation, that it depends where the copy that is seized comes from, doesn't it, as to what it can show? Do you agree with that, Mr. Tusevljak, as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but then I can only speculate as to where this document was seized. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I accept that. All right. Now, can we move from, please, communications generally to the composition of the police in the CSB Sarajevo. You were asked to look, please, at the Defence document which is 1D331, which, I believe, was document number 2 in the bundle that you were handed. No. All right. I think you were asked to look at it, but -- it's obvious I got the wrong note. Yeah, that's the document I want. Now, there is your department -- or there is the setup for May 1992, and as you pointed out, there's yourself for your department and three inspectors. Now, Sasa Blagojevic, was he actually working there in May because you appeared to say that he was in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Sasa Blagojevic was in Gorazde in May. That's what I wrote. His parents took shelter in a village up there, together with his brother, and he went there and he was in that area until the BiH army or the then Territorial Defence took his village and some other villages there and he came back sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I am sorry, but he was working for you, wasn't he? He wasn't working for any other department in any other SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain, he was on my list formally, but physically he was not involved in doing the actual work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then why was he being paid, may I ask, if he wasn't actually doing a stroke of work for you or for the CSB in May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to explain this, wasn't I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all fled Sarajevo, none of us had anything to go on. Nobody even had a pair of shoes, shirts on our backs, a piece of bread, nothing, yet we all had families to look after. And to refuse to grant someone the 65.000 dinars, which was a pitiful sum of money, it would have been an awful thing for me to do, to ask someone to go on working without paying them. None of them even knew at the time where they would be spending the night, didn't have roofs over their heads. From your present standpoint, it's probably difficult for you to understand. I know how I felt at the time. I know the situation of my own family back in April or May. We were shifting between three or four different locations. I had no idea where my two brothers were. My parents had fled to a cottage somewhere in some village or the other. I was trying to make ends meet. I was trying to survive, to fight the next day. The least of all my concerns was the actual policing, the actual police work. It was actually about sheer survival. I think the same applied to everyone else whose names you can see on this list. All the people listed here are refugees and none of them had a chance at the time to stay in their own homes and the same thing applied to their wives and to their children. They were all refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, don't go on, Mr. Tusevljak. It was a simple question. You've now explained for the second time that the payments in April were for, as you put it, humanitarian reasons, and you are saying the same for the payments in May. Is it right also that Mr. Zeljko Rakic did no work for you in May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, he fled Sarajevo with his wife and two children and went to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, stop. Did he do any police work for which he was entitled to payment in May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Petko Pekic do any police work for which he was entitled to payment in May?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he wrote a dispatch or two at the time because he was at the Vraca school.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So in May, none of you, as you've put it, had the slightest interest in police work but got paid for it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did very little actual policing, police work, but yes, we were paid for it. There's another thing, I don't know if we received anything after this salary. If there was another salary, it would have amounted to 5 euro in today's money. So when we talk about the actual amounts, 5 euro, we used this to feed ourselves, to have breakfast, lunch, it was soup-kitchen like. We ate whatever they gave us and we wore whatever we were given. The shirts, the t-shirts, the shoes, or boots or whatever, we -- our own livelihood depended on whether there was a cauldron in which we could cook something. The restaurants weren't operating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Would Your Honours give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course, and I hear the reasons which you give for this, what you have just told the Court was effectively a fraud on the MUP, wasn't it? People being paid for work they had never done? That's right, isn't it, Mr. Tusevljak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree with you altogether. It appears that you are not willing to lend an ear to my reasons. If you want me to go through them again, I'll be happy to do that for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I absolutely do not want you to. You are saying you didn't have anywhere to live, sleep, your families had fled, and all the rest of it, and you needed money, but you were only supposed to be getting money for work done, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless this goes to credibility again, Ms. Korner, do we need to explore this further? The witness has given an explanation. We needn't get sidetracked into this ancillary matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a good reason, Your Honour. It goes to some of the evidence he later gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that by taking payment for work not done, that is a fraud?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to take you back to that time, I'm making an earnest effort, what it was like in 1992. If you want to discuss the features of a potential crime based on the Criminal Code that applied at the time, we can go back to legal matters and discuss that in that framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Tusevljak. I appreciate you say you had reasons for it that you've gone into at length, but I'm simply asking you whether that isn't -- as a police officer who discussed law with Mr. Zecevic, that may be mitigation, you understand the word, but it's actually a criminal offence, isn't it, to claim money for work done when the work has not been done? That's all I'm asking, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because, you see, it would come under the characteristic, wouldn't it, of the sort of disciplinary offence at the very least and criminal offence for which police officers should have been removed, as you've explained?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is May 1992 we are talking about. I'm doing my best to explain that the situation was nothing like February 1992, for example, or even March 1992. I don't know how one of you would have responded in that situation. If you had to go there and see the wife of one of your officers carrying two small children, cradling them in her arms, with nowhere to sleep, no nappies to use, no milk, so if this is fraud, may I then please answer for it. My conscience is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm not going to pursue this any further given your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please -- I only started to deal with the number of people who were actually there. Can we now move, please, to document 20203 at tab 6F. Now, this is the payroll for July at the Romanija-Birac CSB. Could we go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By that stage there's yourself and 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 inspectors? 10 inspectors. There's somebody written in by hand.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but again I need to explain. The only inspector here is me, the chief of the crime unit, Blagojevic, Sasa, inspector. Momcilo Janjetovic is also an inspector. He was head of the white collar crime unit. And Ljubinko Mitrovic, those are the only inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, why are they -- sorry. What are the rest of them, then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandic, Branko, KDZ. Seslija, Miro, KDZ. Savic, Dragan, forensics. Lazic, Savka, Milosevic, Slavko, KDZ. And Sekula Micic, forensics. Mirjana Regoje, secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where do you see that? I can't see that for the moment. The last name. Right. Well, first of all, what is KDZ, I forget?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: KDZ, anti-sabotage protection. If there is a device that is found that didn't go off, then these are the people sent out. The protection people, as we call them, who go to the scene to dismantle the explosive. Or if an area needs checking for explosive devices --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't need -- I just wanted to know what it stood for, thank you very much. I don't need an explanation of what the anti-terrorist lot do. Why are they all shown, then, as inspectors when you say they are not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who typed this up, but if you look at their appointment decisions when they were appointed to their posts, it should be easy enough to tell what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure you got them, but never mind that. If they are not inspectors why are they all signing as inspectors, because everyone seems to sign for these salaries? Forget that, you can't answer that question as to why they didn't change. All right. So out of this --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forget that. No, it was a silly question. I don't see how you can answer it, because you don't know why they would have signed without changing their designation. So out of these listed nine people or eight people plus one secretary, no, nine people, you say four of them worked for you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the others worked for me too. They just weren't inspectors. They were from the anti-sabotage units or from the forensics, but I was their superior as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, can we just run through the ones -- was Mr. Blagojevic actually working for you at the CSB in July?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, he didn't even sign for the salary. His signature is not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's not an answer. Was he working for you at the CSB in July?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, if he had been there, if he had not been in Gorazde, he would have signed up for the salary, which he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, he may not have signed it but it's ticked, and I think if we added it all up we'd find it came to 543.500 dinar. Whether he signed for it or not, are you -- are you saying he never took the salary this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this huge tick here, it starts next to my name and then goes all the way down to the last name almost.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was someone who did this on behalf of the whole crime police unit. Someone picked up the whole sum on behalf of the unit. I'm not sure whose signature that is. And then this someone distributed the salaries to the people who put their names there, who signed here, and the same applies to the lower half of the document. Someone did this on behalf of the entire department. These people didn't go one by one to the mat fin to pick up their salaries. Only one person went, picked up the entire amount and then divvied up whoever he could find.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, are you saying it was this person who then obtained the signatures where we can see them to the side? The person who picked up all the money? Or are you saying that all the signatures are done by one person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this person got the money and then whoever they could track down, whoever they could give their salaries to, these people would then sign for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't appear to have signed for it, does that mean you didn't get the money?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. My salary is not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry, it's got you down --

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just looking at it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's got you down to get 19.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know, but at the time I think this amounted to a grand total of 10 Deutschemark, 5 euro.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What it may amount -- we've heard a number of -- no, Mr. Tusevljak, just wait, please. We've heard a number of people describe how much the dinar was worth. Forgetting what its actual worth was, did you or did you not take your salary at that month?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, my signature isn't there. I couldn't possibly have been given the money until I signed for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, didn't you go and say "where is my money" to this bloke, whoever it was, who picked up the money?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. If I collected a salary, I would have signed for it like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do we understand that Mr. Blagojevic, whether or not he picked up his money, was still not at the centre and still with his family in Gorazde in July?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask that this be marked and admitted, please. I am sorry, it hasn't got a translation, I'm not sure it needs them because all the documents are the same of these mat fin ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We object, Your Honours, for the same reasons as we articulated yesterday. I don't need, I believe, to explain again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the importance of this document is that it shows on the face of it and apparently accurately in some respects who was said to be working in the CSB at the time. And this is obviously -- in this particular department at a time when it is being said they had insufficient manpower to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor produced the chart. It was given to the witness. It lists all the people. We agreed with that. It lists all the people with the explanation, who are the inspectors, who are other people, whether they are KDZ or something else. It was the document that we saw earlier this morning. So if this document is for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Zecevic, that -- well, we aren't going to revisit the arguments that we had yesterday about "fresh evidence," but this is a document which is -- which must be read alongside the document which you referred, and it's something which the Chamber is going to have to assess at the end of the exercise. And as I understand, even if one were to accept fully the witness's explanation about the means of covering persons in pallor circumstances, what Ms. Korner is relying on is that whatever the motive was, you had this list of persons, so therefore that qualifies anything else in the chart. And to that extent it seems to me that it's relevant and indeed probative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I want -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know why it should be MFI'd, unless Your Honours want me to get a translation of it. I don't think it's required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't think a translation is necessary. So it will be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours -- do Your Honours want to take -- I'm going to ask one more document on this topic and then I see that it's time for the adjournment more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... in two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Try to. Could we have a look please at 20172. That's document 20 in our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is August now. "List of workers," and I emphasise, "who performed duties in the CSB in August 1992 and who need to be paid for this month."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the second page in B/C/S. And it's the third page in English. I don't know why we had this one translated and not the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's virtually the same list as July, Mr. Tusevljak. On this occasion, however, did you sign for your 21.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagojevic sign for his 19.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Blagojevic by then actually working for your department?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he started working, as I said, he left for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the month but I think by this time he had left already. August perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In July he is still in Gorazde. In August he is actually in Zvornik, so he is not working for you either in August?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was on my list. I think Sasa Blagojevic sent us one or two or three reports about touring those police stations. There's a report from Vlasenica. I think he was present during inspections in Zvornik, something do with some crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so again, just remind us, please, of this list which appears to show you as having 3, 6, 9 -- 10 inspectors. Which are the ones that actually worked for you? Just give us the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Your Honours, may that also be admitted and marked. And that's the end of this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you would wish to record your objection for the record, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we take the morning break, return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, just a couple of other questions on this business of who was actually working at the CSB. The last document we looked at, which has just been admitted, the August payroll is signed off by Mr. Cvijetic. I don't know if it's on the screen or not. It's gone. It doesn't matter. Did Mr. Cvijetic know that people who were receiving payment weren't actually working?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We need to go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stated all those whose names are on the list, with the exception of Sasa Blagojevic who was in Zvornik, worked in the Security Services Centre, which means that they performed their functions. However, I would like to emphasise that there is only one general crime prevention inspector here and two white collar crime inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, you misunderstand me. We can see definitely that Mr. Cvijetic signed off on this salary payroll, sorry, I'm not sure of on the earlier ones, but Mr. Cvijetic would have to sign, wouldn't he, to say that the people should receive the payment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When Mr. Cvijetic signed off, would he have known that, for example, going back to July or earlier, that the people who were receiving payment would not have actually worked? For example, let's take Mr. Blagojevic in Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. He knew about it. We discussed it and he also knew the reasons for which they received their salaries and he absolutely agreed with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this something also that Mico Stanisic, as the minister present in the complex, would have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the basis for that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking it. I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the basis for the fact that Mico Stanisic was present in the complex, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm asking the question. If I'm not allowed to ask the question, then I'm not allowed to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you should establish first whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought the present in the complex was parenthetical, but I would have assumed the basis of the question is as the minister by ordinary ministerial responsibility. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. Your Honour, I don't see any reason for giving the basis of the question, but clearly the ministerial responsibility to his paymasters, if nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tusevljak, would Mr. Stanisic as the minister have known this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you see, you've told us that Mr. Cvijetic discussed matters with the minister, wouldn't he have had to discuss something as important as that with the minister?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only an assumption. I know what were the topics of my conversations with Mr. Cvijetic, but what he spoke about with the minister, I wouldn't know, because I was not present at any of their discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you -- I am sorry, Mr. Cvijetic [sic], you gave evidence, and I'll come back to that later, earlier, that Mr. Cvijetic had informed you about his discussions with the minister and that's how you knew about it, and I'll come back to the actual matter that was discussed. Now, was it right, from your dealings with Mr. Cvijetic, that matters of importance he had to raise with the minister?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was important matters, I assume that probably Zoran Cvijetic had to discuss it with the minister. However, about this specific topic, I know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say you assume. Mr. Cvijetic told you, didn't he, that he would discuss matters with the minister?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some matters, yes, but this particular matter, I don't know whether Mr. Cvijetic spoke to the minister about the salaries and payrolls. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware, if you weren't say no, that there was considerable discussion about how the MUP was to be financed altogether, discussion in government circles?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. At the time I had absolutely no possibility to follow the discussions within the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And one final question which may seem slightly out of context, which it is, did you by any chance know a man named Kenan Delic, an inspector who worked at Sarajevo airport?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was the assistant or the deputy commander of the traffic police station before the war, and even before that he used to an inspector in charge of aliens, foreigners, but I think that that might be him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So he was a obviously a Muslim with a name like that; is that right? Or maybe not.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say he worked -- sorry. Sorry. Was that that he was at the airport or not? You say he was the assistant or deputy commander of the traffic police station. Is that at the airport?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the traffic police. Possibly the airport police. I know him from the time when he was inspector in charge of aliens in the city SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I move, please, to the question of these Golf investigations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we move on to the Golf incidents, could I just ask the witness about one thing relating to this matter of having people on the payroll who actually did not work for the MUP, because I'm curious to know and I'm trying to understand how this came about. Was Mr. Cvijetic's reasons to allow payment to people who he knew did no longer work for the MUP, did he do so out of -- out of what really? What was his reasons? Why was it so widely accepted apparently that it was legitimate or considered to be legitimate to continue to pay people although they were no longer working? What was the underlying understanding of this? Are you able to clarify and do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking here about the very beginning of the war, April, May, and June, and we are also talking about two or mostly three names. The reasons were exclusively humanitarian. Mr. Cvijetic or myself or Drago Borovcanin, who was chief of the police department, considered that this was the only way to provide at least some assistance to those people. If you look at subsequent payrolls, beginning in September and onwards, you will not find a single person not actually performing work, so you have to bear in mind that the payrolls have changed. In April, May and June we have certain names on the payrolls and the underlying reason was that those people, who left all their property in Sarajevo and left with their families and arrived on the territory controlled by Republika Srpska, who were without any accommodation and in big trouble, they needed some help in order to overcome this personal crisis. Those people who did not work in the MUP later on were removed from payrolls and then later on they did not receive any salaries. So the only reason for all this was purely humanitarian. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. This clarifies a part of the question that I had. The remaining part of my question is whether the people who now suddenly found themselves with no home and no jobs and no means of subsistence, were they old MUP members? I mean, were they offered this option because of their previous engagement with the MUP or would it also sometimes include, say, a friend who had nothing to do with the MUP but who just happened to find himself or herself in very unfortunate circumstances and who were then being offered some assistance by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They are all employees of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They all belonged to the BiH MUP. And then they left it either on the 4th of April or subsequently they were driven out from the MUP. And then they arrived in the territory under the control of Republika Srpska. So they are all former employees of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is not a single person on the list who was not the member of the police before the war broke out. It's only them. Only they received some money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Back to you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal with the topic -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to deal now, Mr. Tusevljak, with the topic of these thefts of the Golfs from the TAS factory in Vogosca. I think it's right that over the course of the months that these investigations went on, something like more than 100 police officers were involved in these investigations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was 100 policemen. Not nearly that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'll check but I have a feeling that's the number that you gave us when you were interviewed, but I'll check that and come back to it. And there were two major reasons, weren't there, why this investigation was actually ordered by the highest levels, wasn't it, and the government itself?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we received the assignment from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'll show you a document in a minute that shows you it went as high as the government, but, first, the cars that were stolen, there were a lot of them and they were valuable cars, that's right, isn't it? All brand new Golfs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that was the reason. The vehicles were brand new.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And although originally it appears that the factory had been attacked by the Bosniaks or the army of ABiH, whatever, the TO, I think, they didn't take very many, we'll look at the report, and thereafter, because Vogosca was taken over by the Serbs, the factory fell into Serb hands. And that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And of course if it had remained, if all the Golfs hadn't been stolen like this, that represented a valuable source of income, didn't it, for the government of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if the factory which had produced all these brand new Golfs now came into possession of the Serbian -- the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the sale of those cars represented quite a large amount of income for the government, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the government sold them, then, of course, they were valuable vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the other part of this was that it was a major public scandal, wasn't it, that these Golfs were being driven to Serbia, for example?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not sure what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, on the face of it, why so much time was spent investigating these thefts. Not only time but manpower. And one of the other aspects was that it would appear that government ministers were helping themselves to these cars; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that some of the vehicles were registered as belonging to the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just have a look at some of the documents on this, please. Could you please have a look at 1D82, which is document 12 in the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault, 1D182, sorry, not 82. 1D182. In fact, it may also be in the Defence bundle, because I think you looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it would be helpful, it's document number 2 in Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think Mr. Tusevljak can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is the note already on the 16th of July which you made, if we go to the second page, together with Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Go back to the first page, did you actually go down to Vogosca to do this or did you just make the note from the information provided by Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I went to Vogosca myself, together with Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see that the description that the factory had been apparently attacked by Green Berets on the 17th or thereabouts in April, and then thereafter had been taken over by the Serb -- Serbs but had not been properly secured. And then if we go down to the second -- sorry, the third paragraph, the last sentence -- first of all it says that on 20th of June, the War Presidency had passed a decision prohibiting the taking of the vehicles, then Mr. Tintor -- before that, Mr. Tintor had agreed that vehicles could be taken. And then finally this: Kopravica said before the War Presidency passed the decision, he had ordered, and by "he" it's, I think, meant to be Mr. Tintor, six Golf vehicles be given for the needs of the government of the SR -- of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the vehicles were sent directly to the prime minister. So that's the information that you got at that stage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this Official Note we simply wrote down the factual situation as told to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this was sent to the CSB, but was this something of sufficient importance that it would have gone to the minister?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This went to the chief of the Security Services Centre. Whether he forwarded it, I don't know, but this was written for the chief of the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you told us that at these collegium meetings that were held every morning, matters of importance were discussed and you saw documents and reports that were going to go to the minister because they were discussed. Was this one of them that was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was discussed and this document was probably drafted at the request of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And when it was discussed, did Mr. Cvijetic say, right, we'll send this up to the minister himself because these thefts are such a major crime?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska is informed, it is always important to specify whether it goes straight to the minister or to some of the departments or services. It could have been sent to the police department or some other department or personally to the minister, but it is impossible for me to establish this without the cover letter that would have been sent to Sarajevo. So it's only the covering letter where you can find the information about to whom the chief of the centre said this. If it did go to the ministry, it is probable that the minister himself would have been apprised of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can you have a look at one shortly after which is, please, 1D93 at tab 17A of the Prosecution bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is - if we go to the second page, please, in the B/C/S/ and English - a document signed by Mr. Macar. Is that the gentleman to whom you reported?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of the administration. He wasn't co-ordinator yet, he was chief of administration at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I am sorry, I believe the witness should repeat his answer because it wasn't recorded as he said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was recorded quite differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The question was: Was Mr. Macar the man to whom you reported, could you repeat your answer quite slowly, please, so that we get the correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we submitted our reports to Planojevic, who was chief of the crime prevention administration, and within this administration Goran Macar was only a co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And when Dobrivoje Planojevic left his post, when he was replaced, it was then that Goran Macar was appointed to that post but I'm not sure in which month it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, this document is sent to the chiefs of 13 SJBs that came within the purview of the CSB Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the first page again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can see that the crime prevention administration sent the dispatch directly to the police stations and the CSB of Romanija-Birac received this dispatch only as an information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So this was at that stage being taken up by someone who was at the headquarters of the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, the crime prevention administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move then, please, to 1D83, tab 24. Sorry, I've done it again, 1D183. I keep leaving out the 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just stay there for a moment -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just stay there for a moment. Who is Pero Vujicic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Vujicic was an old member of the state security service. I think he worked in the analytics department before the war, and in the Republika Srpska MUP, I think that at the beginning he was in the office of the minister and later on chief of the analytical department. He may have stayed on that post until the end of the war but I'm not quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page -- [Microphone not activated] -- in English and in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document again addressed -- this is a document addressed again to the SJBs and also to you for information and this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the last page, please, again, on each. Again, Mr. Macar, and if you go back to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A few days after his last -- it's about, well, a week, maybe eight days, he is actually reminding the SJB chiefs about the TAS information he wants, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an urgent document. They are asking them to respond quickly, and it's pursuant to the same dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So clearly from your knowledge of the procedures --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was recorded: "This is an urgent document. They are asking him to respond quickly, and it's pursuant to the same dispatch." That is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just repeat your answer. My question was that Mr. Macar is reminding the SJB chiefs of his dispatch, and what did you say to that? You said it was urgent, an urgent document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it said we have an urgency, meaning that a response should be accelerated to a previously sent out dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So do you agree from your knowledge of these type of dispatches this was considered to be a really important matter?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK [Resumed]
